## Introduction

### Learning goals

In the previous session, you wrote a basic shell script to run FastQC for a single
FASTQ file.
Here, we will finalize that script, and focus on running it many times with loops.
Specifically, you will learn:

- How to add "logging" statements to a shell script
- How `for` loops work
- How to use a `for` loop to loop over files and run a shell script many times
- How to loop over _samples_ (pairs of FASTQ files) using parameter expansion

### Getting ready

1. At <https://ondemand.osc.edu>, start a VS Code session in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`.
2. In the terminal, navigate to your `week07` dir.
3. _Optional: Create a new Markdown file for class notes and save it in your `week07` dir._

## The big picture

The strategy you'll learn is to write scripts that
**run a single program a single time**,
even though you commonly need to run a CLI tool many times,
e.g. separately for each file or sample.
That's because at OSC, you can save a lot of time by
submitting a **separate batch job** for each file or sample,
since these jobs can all run simultaneously^[
It is possible to use another strategy that parallelizes program runs within a
script, but we will use this strategy instead.].

To accommodate this, you will:

- Make your scripts flexible by passing arguments to them
  _(as seen in the previous session)_.
- Loop over files/samples outside of the script,
  and run/submit the script many times _(as you'll see today)_.

As a result, you'll also type important **code outside of your scripts**,
and that code orchestrates your workflow.
You will store that code in **Markdown files**, which then provide a record of what you did.

## Your FastQC script

### The script so far

In the previous session, you wrote the following script to run FastQC,
which should be saved at `scripts/fastqc.sh`:

```{.bash .file filename="scripts/fastqc.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Load the OSC module for FastQC
module load fastqc/0.12.1

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC
fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"
```

Because the script accepts the FASTQ file and output dir as arguments,
it deliberately runs FastQC for only one FASTQ file at a time ---
for example:

```bash
# [Don't run this yet]
bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz results/fastqc
```

Notice that this script consists mostly of boilerplate code, with
**just a single command to run our program of interest.**
Therefore, you can adopt this script as a template for scripts that run other
command-line programs, and will generally only need minor modifications!

### Add some "logging" statements

It is often useful to have your shell script report or "log" what it is doing.
For instance:

- At what date and time was the script run.
- Which arguments were passed to the script.
- What are the designated output dirs/files.
- Perhaps even summaries of the output (we won't do this here).

This information can help with troubleshooting and record-keeping.
One thing to keep in mind here is that later,
when you submit scripts as batch jobs,
such logging output will not be printed to screen but will end up in text files.
Therefore, you can store those text files along with other output files to keep
detailed records of what you did!

Let's add some code to produce logging information to the FastQC script:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Load the OSC module for FastQC
module load fastqc/0.12.1

# Copy the placeholder variables
fastq="$1"
outdir="$2"

# Initial logging
echo "# Starting script fastqc.sh"
date
echo "# Input FASTQ file:   $fastq"
echo "# Output dir:         $outdir"
echo

# Create the output dir if needed
mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Run FastQC
fastqc --outdir "$outdir" "$fastq"

# Final logging
echo
echo "# Used FastQC version:"
fastqc --version
echo
echo "# Successfully finished script fastqc.sh"
date
```

A couple of notes about the lines that were added to the script above:

- A "marker line" `Successfully finished script` indicates that the end of the
  script was reached. This is useful because of your `set` settings:
  seeing this line printed means that **no errors were encountered**.

- Running `date` at the beginning and end of the script is one way to be able to
  see **how long** the script took to run, and to keep a record of **when** it was run.

- Printing the **input file names** can be particularly useful for troubleshooting.

- The lines that only have `echo` will simply print a blank line,
  basically as a separator between sections.

- For scripts that run bioinformatics tools,
  it's a good idea to include a line to **print the program version**.

{{< fa user-edit >}} _Update your `scripts/fastqc.sh` script with the code from the box above._

## A "protocol" Markdown file

The abovementioned loop code _could_ be directly typed in the terminal.
But it is more convenient and reproducible to put this in a Markdown file,
so you will keep a record of your analysis steps.
For small projects, a simple "protocol" could be added to your main `README.md`.
Let's practice with that by writing a README for the current analysis:

```bash
touch README.md
```

Open that file in the VS Code editor, and add the following to it:

````markdown
# RNA-seq data analysis

## General information

- Author: <your name>
- Date: 2026-10-07
- Environment: Pitzer cluster at OSC via VS Code
- Working dir: `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/week07`

## Project background

This project is ...

## Protocol
````

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
In a few weeks, we'll discuss how you can organize this kind of information for
larger projects.
:::

## For loops

Loops are another universal element of programming languages,
and are used to **repeat operations**.
Here, we'll only cover the most common type of loop: the `for` loop.

A `for` loop **iterates** over a collection, such as a list of files,
and allows you to perform one or more actions for each element in the collection.
In the example below,
the collection is just a short list of numbers (`1`, `2`, and `3`):

```bash
for a_number in 1 2 3; do
    echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number"
    echo "--------"
done
```
```bash-out
In this iteration of the loop, the number is 1
--------
In this iteration of the loop, the number is 2
--------
In this iteration of the loop, the number is 3
--------
```

The **indented lines** between `do` and `done` contain the code that is being executed
_as many times as there are items in the collection_:
in this case 3 times, as you can tell from the output above.

Here are two key things to understand about `for` loops:

- In each iteration of the loop, one element in the collection
  **is being assigned to the variable** specified after `for`.
  Above, `a_number` contained `1` in the first iteration,
  `2` in the second, and `3` in the third and last one.

- The loop runs sequentially for each item in the collection,
  and will run exactly as many times as there are items in the collection.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More about `for` loops: what runs under the hood, and syntax _(Click to expand)_

What was actually run under the hood in the example above is the following:

```bash
# (Don't run this)
a_number=1
echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number"
echo "--------"

a_number=2
echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number"
echo "--------"

a_number=3
echo "In this iteration of the loop, the number is $a_number"
echo "--------"
```

On the first and last, unindented lines,
`for` loops contain the following mandatory keywords:

| Keyword | Purpose	                            |
|---------|-------------------------------------|
| `for`	  | After `for`, we set the **variable name** (an arbitrary name; above we used `a_number`)
| `in`	  | After `in`, we specify the **collection** (list of items) we are looping over
| `do`	  | After `do`, we have one or more lines specifying what to do with each item
| `done`  | Tells the shell we are done with the loop

: {.striped .hover}

:::

#### Combining loops and globbing

An extremely common strategy is to loop over files with globbing, for example:

```bash
for fastq_file in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do
    echo "# Running an analysis on $fastq_file"
    # [This is where you would put additional commands to process each FASTQ file]
done
```
```bash-out
# Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
# Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
# Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
# Running an analysis on ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: What will these loops print?

Given these files:

```bash
mkdir -p sandbox
touch sandbox/file1.txt sandbox/S1_R1.fastq.gz sandbox/S1_R2.fastq.gz
```

- What do you expect the output of this loop to be?

  ```bash
  for file in sandbox/*fastq.gz; do
      echo "I have found file $file"
  done
  ```

  <!----
  <details><summary>_Click for the solution_</summary><p>
  The glob only matches the two FASTQ files, so the loop runs twice:

  ```bash-out
  I have found file sandbox/S1_R1.fastq.gz
  I have found file sandbox/S1_R2.fastq.gz
  ```
  </p></details>
  ---->

- And of this loop?

  ```bash
  for file in sandbox/f*; do
      echo "$f"
  done
  ```

  <!----
  <details><summary>_Click for the solution_</summary><p>
  Look closely: the loop variable is `file`, but the `echo` line uses `$f` --
  a variable that was never assigned.
  Because we're at the interactive prompt rather than in a script with
  `set -u`, the shell doesn't complain about the unset variable --
  it just silently treats it as an empty string.
  So the loop prints one empty line for each matching file ---
  here, that is just `file1.txt`.

  This is exactly the kind of silent failure that `set -u` protects you
  from: in a script with strict Bash settings, this typo would cause an
  immediate error instead of silently doing the wrong thing.
  </p></details>
  ---->
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
### Why is there "`; do`" in a `for` loop? _(Click to expand)_

You may find the `; do` at the end of the first line of the `for` loop to be odd.
What is that all about?

First, a semicolon is a way to enter multiple commands on a single line --
for example, the line below would first run `ls` and then `echo "Hello"`:

```bash
ls; echo "Hello"
```

_(So, `;` can be thought of as a counterpart to `\`, which allows you to spread a single command_
_across multiple lines: with a `;`, you can have multiple commands on a single line.)_

As such, you could also write `for` loops like so...

```bash
for file in sandbox/*fastq.gz
do
    echo "$file"
done
```

...and some people prefer that variant.
You can do it either way, but we will continue to demonstrate the `; do` variant.
:::

## Running a script many times with a loop

You will now loop over all FASTQ files in the `../garrigos/fastq` dir,
and run your `fastqc.sh` script for each file.
Add the following to your `README.md` file,
and then run the code inside the code block:

````markdown
### Step 1 - Run FastQC for each FASTQ file:

```bash
for fastq in ../garrigos/fastq/*fastq.gz; do
    bash scripts/fastqc.sh "$fastq" results/fastqc
done
```
````

```bash-out
# Starting script fastqc.sh
Thu Sep 25 13:58:21 EDT 2025
# Input FASTQ file:   ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
# Output dir:         results/fastqc

Started analysis of S63_R1.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]

# Successfully finished script fastqc.sh
Thu Sep 25 13:58:26 EDT 2025

# Starting script fastqc.sh
Thu Sep 25 13:58:26 EDT 2025
# Input FASTQ file:   ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
# Output dir:         results/fastqc

Started analysis of S63_R2.fastq.gz
Approx 5% complete for S63_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
```

That produces a lot of output!
You can hopefully see that this looping approach is quite powerful,
allowing you to easily run a script many times.

However, note that this runs the `fastqc.sh` script _sequentially_:
after it was run for the first FASTQ file, it will run for the second file,
and so on.
If these had been full-size FASTQ files,
it may have still taken hours for this to finish.
So, while you have now learned an elegant way to run a script many times,
you have not yet learned how to run it simultaneously in parallel.
In week 9, you'll learn about submitting scripts like this as batch jobs,
so they can be run simultaneously, which saves a lot of time.

## Looping over samples

FastQC is run separately for each FASTQ file,
but many tools that process paired-end data need the R1 and R2 files of a sample
_together_.
Such tools should be run once per sample, i.e. once per _pair_ of FASTQ files.

A common way to do this is to loop over the **R1 files only**,
and to "infer" the name of the corresponding R2 file inside the loop.
That works because the R1 and R2 file names should be identical except for
the read-direction identifier (typically `_R1`/`_R2`).

### Parameter expansion

To infer the R2 file name, you can search-and-replace text in a variable's value
with "parameter expansion":

```bash
fastq_R1=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
fastq_R2=${fastq_R1/_R1/_R2}

echo "$fastq_R2"
```
```bash-out
../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
```

The syntax is `${var_name/<search>/<replace>}`:
you reference the variable with curly braces, then add a forward slash and the
search pattern, and then another forward slash and the replacement.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Search for `_R1` and not just `R1`:
in other datasets, the string "R1" may also occur in the sample ID
(e.g. `ERR1234`)!
:::

### A per-sample loop

Here is a loop that runs once per sample, and prints the two file names for each:

```bash
for R1 in ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    R2=${R1/_R1/_R2}
    echo "# R1 file: $R1"
    echo "# R2 file: $R2"
done
```
```bash-out
# R1 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
# R2 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
# R1 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R1.fastq.gz
# R2 file: ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R2.fastq.gz
# [...output truncated...]
```

To run a script for each sample, you would replace the `echo` lines with a call
to a script that accepts both files as arguments, for example:

```bash
# [Don't run this - the trimgalore.sh script doesn't exist yet]
for R1 in ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    R2=${R1/_R1/_R2}
    bash scripts/trimgalore.sh "$R1" "$R2" results/trimgalore
done
```

In [next week's exercises](../week08/w8_exercises.qmd),
you'll write such a script for the program TrimGalore and run it with this kind of loop.

In this lecture,
you've seen an example of using a shell script to run a CLI bioinformatics tool.
You've also learned how to write and use `for` loops,
both to loop over files and to loop over samples.

The [self-study page with shell tips and tricks](./w7c_tricks.qmd)
goes into more detail on parameter expansion,
and also covers command substitution, `basename`, and renaming files with loops.

And in week 9, we'll move on to submitting shell scripts as batch jobs at OSC.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More about the "hard-coding" of settings _(Click to expand)_

We've been writing shell scripts that accept arguments,
instead of including variable things like inputs and outputs in the scripts themselves.
The latter method can be referred to as "hard-coding" these items.

You can also use arguments for _settings_ like bioinformatics program options
you may want to vary among different runs of the script,
or relatedly, for information about your data like read length.
If you don't hard-code these options in your script but have arguments for them,
it is easier to re-use your script in different contexts.

But there is a balance to be struck,
and you can also "hobble" your script with a confusing array of arguments.
When you do hard-code potentially variable things in your script,
you may want to clearly define them **at the top of your script**.
For example:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Settings and constants
MIN_QUAL=30
```

Another applicable example is when you use an Apptainer container in your script.
It can be a good idea to define the URL or path to the container as a variable
at the top of your script:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Settings and constants
FASTQC_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.12.1--104d26ddd9519960
```

Such variables can be referred to as "constants",
since they are hard-coded in the script.
In shell code, ALL-CAPS is regularly used for them^[
But this is far from universal. It is also fairly common to use all-caps
for all shell variables, but this is not what we've been doing.].
:::
